auth.setupHint: Find the one-time setup token in the server logs.
auth.socketWarning: Nautix controls the Docker socket, which is equivalent to root on this host. Keep it bound to localhost.
auth.otherSessions: Your other sessions (other browsers or devices) will be signed out.

topology.paletteHint: Drag onto a network box, or onto the canvas for an external service.
topology.internalHint: Containers on an isolated network cannot reach the outside world and cannot be reached from it.
topology.externalHint: Not on any shared network. Published ports bind to 127.0.0.1 only.
topology.sharesNetwork: Containers inside a box share its network.
topology.exposeWarning: Anyone who can reach this machine can reach this port. Put a reverse proxy with auth in front instead.
topology.inspectorEmpty: Select a container or a network to inspect it.
topology.removeNetworkBody: The network will be deleted. It has no containers.
topology.networkNotEmpty: Move or remove its containers first.
topology.removeContainerBody: This deletes the container ({{image}}). Its volumes are kept.
topology.joinHint: A container on two networks bridges them: use it for a reverse proxy that must reach isolated services.
topology.empty: No containers yet. Drag something from the palette.
topology.exportEnvWarning: Values may contain passwords. Without this, variables are written as ${NAME} placeholders.
topology.resetLayoutBody: Saved positions are discarded and boxes and containers go back to the automatic arrangement.
topology.restartHint: Use “no” for one-shot containers (like hello-world) or they restart forever.
topology.commandHint: Replaces the image's default command. Quotes are supported.
topology.saveTemplate: Save to the panel for reuse
topology.templateHint: Ports, variables and volumes are stored on this server, including variable values.
topology.templateIntro: Templates are saved in Nautix and appear in this panel under "My images"; drag or click them to deploy with these defaults.
topology.healthcheckHint: Runs inside the container every 30 s; exit code 0 means healthy.
topology.createOnly: Create only, do not start (docker create)
topology.fixedIpHint: Inside {{subnet}}. Leave empty and Docker picks one; it can change if the container is recreated.
topology.copyHint: Built-in templates cannot be changed. This saves your own version under "My images" with the values below; the original stays as it is.
topology.kindOverlayHint: One network over every server of the swarm: services find each other by name wherever they run.
topology.overlayEncryptedHint: Recommended. Docker leaves it off by default and the traffic then travels in the clear.
topology.overlayAttachableHint: Also lets standalone containers (docker run) join, not only services.

images.removeBody: {{name}} will be deleted from this host.
images.credentialsNote: Leave empty to use the login saved in Settings → Registries. Credentials typed here are sent once to the engine and are not stored or logged.
images.loadHint: A .tar produced by docker save. Its images are added to this host.
images.importHint: A .tar of a root filesystem; it becomes a single-layer image.

volumes.title: Volumes
volumes.removeBody: All data stored in this volume will be lost. This cannot be undone.
volumes.browseHint: Nautix mounts the volume in a short-lived helper container with no network. Downloads and uploads are recorded in the audit log.
volumes.notReadable: This file cannot be read as text.
volumes.uploadReplaces: Files with the same name in this folder are replaced.
volumes.uploadOwner: The files are created owned by root. If the app that uses this volume runs as another user, it may not be able to read or change them.
volumes.uploadInUse: A container uses this volume. Changing files under a running app, a database above all, can corrupt its data: stop it first.
volumes.upload_tooLarge: Too much at once: the limit is 256 MB per upload.
volumes.upload_nameTooLong: A file name is longer than 100 bytes and cannot be uploaded.

settings.title: Settings
settings.tokenShownOnce: Copy this token now. It will not be shown again.
settings.revokeBody: Anything using it will stop working immediately.
settings.roleHint: Viewers can look but not change anything, and cannot open terminals or see environment values.
settings.tlsOff: Nautix is serving plain HTTP. Set NAUTIX_TLS=auto (the compose file does) to enable HTTPS and manage the certificate here.
settings.tlsExternal: The certificate is loaded from files given in the environment; change those files and restart Nautix.
settings.tlsHostsHint: localhost, 127.0.0.1 and ::1 are always included. Add the names or IPs you open Nautix with, comma separated.
settings.tlsTrustTitle: How to make the browser trust it
settings.tlsTrustWindows: Windows: double-click the file → Install certificate → Local machine → Trusted Root Certification Authorities. Restart the browser.
settings.tlsTrustMac: macOS: open the file in Keychain Access, then set it to Always Trust.
settings.tlsTrustLinux: Linux/WSL: copy it to /usr/local/share/ca-certificates/nautix.crt and run update-ca-certificates. If the browser runs on Windows, use the Windows step.
settings.tlsTrustFirefox: Firefox keeps its own store: Settings → Privacy → Certificates → Import (or enable security.enterprise_roots.enabled).
settings.registriesHint: Saved logins are used to pull and push images without typing credentials.
settings.registryStored: Nautix checks the login with the registry first, then keeps the password encrypted (AES-256-GCM) in its data volume. It is never shown again.
settings.registryRemoveBody: Pulls and pushes to this registry will need credentials again.
settings.backupHint: Downloads everything Nautix stores: users, tokens, layout, templates, Compose projects, gateway routes, saved registry logins, the encryption key and certificates.
settings.backupWarning: The file contains secrets and the key that opens them. Keep it as private as a password.
settings.restoreBody: Nautix will restart and replace its current data with the backup. The current data is kept in a before-restore folder inside the data volume. You will have to sign in again.
settings.resetPasswordWarning: The user is signed out everywhere and must use the new password. Tell them through a private channel.
settings.auditNote: Changes name what was touched (container, variable names, ports, bindings, rules) but never a value. Reading a container's settings or a zone document is recorded once every ten minutes per person.

compose.title: Compose projects
compose.deleteBody: Only the saved file is deleted. Containers it started keep running until you bring the project down.
compose.inspectorEmpty: Select a service or a network box. Drag templates from the palette to add services.
compose.noNetworks: No networks defined yet. Create one with “New network”.
compose.publicHint: Published on all interfaces. Use 127.0.0.1:host:container to keep it private.
compose.removeServiceBody: It is removed from the file, together with references to it in depends_on.
compose.removeNetworkBody: The network is removed from the file and from every service that used it.
compose.defaultBoxHint: Services that name no network share this implicit network, as Docker Compose does.
compose.riskBody: These settings give containers broad control over this machine. Continue only if you trust the images.
compose.downBody: Containers and networks of this project are stopped and removed.

issue.duplicateContainerName: Container name “{{name}}” is also used by {{other}}

issue.publicPort: Port {{port}} is published on all interfaces

issue.relativeBind: “{{volume}}” is a relative path; use an absolute host path or a named volume
issue.dockerSocket: Mounts the Docker socket (full control of the host)

tunnel.handle: Drag to another box to open a tunnel
tunnel.title: Tunnel
tunnel.explain: Only port {{port}} of the target crosses between the two networks; everything else stays isolated. Nothing is published on the host.
tunnel.removeBody: Containers in {{from}} will no longer reach the service in {{to}} through it.
tunnel.intro: Containers in “{{from}}” will be able to reach one port of a container in “{{to}}”. A small forwarder (socat) joins both networks and relays only that TCP port.
tunnel.noTargets: There are no containers in “{{network}}” to open a tunnel to.
tunnel.listenHint: Port other containers use. Defaults to the target port.
tunnel.scope: Everything in “{{from}}” will be able to connect to this tunnel on port {{port}}, not only one container.

details.noChanges: No changes compared with the image.
details.pathHint: Absolute directory or file inside the container
details.filesNote: Uploads are extracted into the directory above (max 256 MB). Admins only.
details.commitNote: The container is paused while its filesystem is captured.
details.isTunnel: This container is a tunnel between two networks.
details.ipsStopped: A stopped container has no address. Start it to see it.
details.ipsHint: Other containers on the same network reach it by this address (or by its name). To point your own domain at it,
details.fixIpBody: A fixed address stays the same when the container restarts, so a domain pointed at it keeps working.
details.fixIpWarning: Nautix reconnects the container to this network to apply it: connections through this network drop for a moment.
details.historyNote: Changes to this container's environment, ports and bindings, and who read its settings. Variable names only, never values.

system.title: System
system.pruneIntro: See exactly what would be deleted before anything is removed. Nothing changes until you confirm.
system.allImages: Also remove unused images (not only untagged ones)
system.confirmBody: {{count}} items will be deleted. This cannot be undone.
system.cleanupIntro: Like docker system prune, but you choose: every unused item is listed below with its own checkbox. Nothing is removed until you confirm.
system.cleanupVolumes: Also include unused volumes (they hold data)
system.cleanupVolumesWarn: A volume that nothing uses may still hold data you want. Check the list before deleting.
system.cleanupNoCache: The build cache that docker system prune also clears is not included here.

gateway.title: Gateways and proxies
gateway.none: No supported gateway or proxy found. Drag Kong, Nginx, Caddy, Traefik or HAProxy from the palette into a network box (publish its traffic port, and 8001 too for Kong) and it will show up here.
gateway.intro: Map a path and/or a domain to a service. Nautix saves the mappings and applies them to the gateway for you; no config files or curl needed. Pick a service the gateway can reach (same network, or a tunnel) or type any URL.
gateway.failed: The gateway did not accept the routes
gateway.noProxyPort: Publish port {{port}} of the gateway on the host to get a ready-to-use test command.
gateway.noUpstreamPath: {{name}} forwards to a host and port only: destinations like http://service:80/base (with a path) are not accepted. Kong does accept them.
gateway.supported: Supported: Kong, Nginx, Caddy, Traefik and HAProxy.
gateway.lockout: Your address ({{address}}) is not in this list: you would not be able to use this route from here.
gateway.allowNote: Empty = anyone who can reach the gateway. Entries are addresses or networks such as 10.0.0.0/24. Behind another proxy or Docker's port forwarding, the gateway may see that proxy's address instead of the client's.

how.kong: Routes are posted to Kong's admin API.
how.nginx: Nautix writes the file 00-nautix.conf in the container, checks it with nginx -t and reloads nginx.
how.caddy: Nautix writes the Caddyfile in the container, validates it and reloads Caddy.
how.traefik: Nautix writes /etc/traefik/dynamic/nautix.yml; Traefik watches that folder, so there is nothing to reload.
how.haproxy: Nautix writes haproxy.cfg in the container, checks it and reloads HAProxy.

keep.kong: Kong keeps routes in memory: after the gateway restarts, press “Apply again”.
keep.nginx: The file lives inside the container: it survives a restart, but if you recreate the container press “Apply again”.
keep.caddy: The Caddyfile lives inside the container: it survives a restart, but if you recreate the container press “Apply again”.
keep.traefik: The file is kept in the data volume of the Traefik template, so it survives restarts and recreation. With no routes saved, Traefik answers 404 to everything.
keep.haproxy: The file is kept in the template's volume, so it survives restarts and recreation.

failedHintFor.kong: Check that the container is running, that it is on a user-defined network and that its admin API listens on 0.0.0.0:8001 (the Kong template does).
failedHintFor.nginx: Check that the container is running and on a user-defined network. The new file was not kept if nginx -t found an error: the output above says which line.
failedHintFor.caddy: Check that the container is running and on a user-defined network. A Caddyfile that does not validate is not applied: the output above says why.
failedHintFor.traefik: Check that the container is running and that the template's data volume is mounted at /etc/traefik/dynamic.
failedHintFor.haproxy: Check that the container is running and on a user-defined network. A configuration that does not validate is not applied: the output above says why.

builds.title: Builds
builds.intro: Write a Dockerfile, check it against Nautix's rules and build an image on this engine. Extra files you add below are the build context.
builds.argsWarning: Build arguments are stored in the image history: never put secrets here.
builds.filesHint: Small text files the Dockerfile can COPY (package.json, nginx.conf, ...).
builds.noCache: Do not use the build cache
builds.blocked: Fix the errors above to build.

rules.NX-DF001: Base image {{image}} is not pinned to a version; builds will change over time.
rules.NX-DF002: The container runs as root. Add a USER instruction with an unprivileged user.
rules.NX-DF003: No HEALTHCHECK: Docker cannot tell whether the app is actually working.
rules.NX-DF004: ADD for a local file: COPY is clearer and has no surprises.
rules.NX-DF005: {{name}} looks like a secret and would be saved in the image. Pass it at run time instead.
rules.NX-DF006: Piping a download into a shell runs unverified code during the build.
rules.NX-DF007: apt-get update on its own gets cached and goes stale; run it together with install.
rules.NX-DF008: apt-get install without --no-install-recommends adds unneeded packages.
rules.NX-DF009: WORKDIR {{path}} is relative; use an absolute path.
rules.NX-DF010: More than one {{keyword}} in the same stage: only the last one counts.
rules.NX-DF011: The file must start with FROM (only ARG may come before it).
rules.NX-DF013: {{keyword}} in shell form: the app does not receive stop signals. Use the ["exec", "form"].
rules.NX-DF014: Copying everything before restoring dependencies reinstalls them on every code change. Copy only the dependency files first.
rules.NX-DF015: {{keyword}} comes after CMD/ENTRYPOINT. It works, but the file reads better with build steps first.

blocks.dropHere: Drop here to move it to the end of this stage
blocks.emptyBody: A Dockerfile starts with FROM. Add a stage, then add instructions to it, or pick "Containerize my app" above.
blocks.commandHint: Several lines become one RUN joined with \\.
blocks.healthNone: Disable the base image's health check

kw.FROM: Start a stage from a base image
kw.ADD: Copy files or download a URL / unpack an archive
kw.ENV: Set environment variables (kept in the image)
kw.WORKDIR: Folder where the next steps run
kw.EXPOSE: Document the ports the app listens on
kw.HEALTHCHECK: How Docker checks the app works
kw.VOLUME: Folder meant to hold persistent data
kw.LABEL: Metadata for the image
kw.STOPSIGNAL: Signal sent to stop the container
kw.ONBUILD: Instruction that runs when this image is used as a base
kw.OTHER: An instruction Nautix has no form for: edit it as text.

tip.FROM: Every stage starts here. Use a specific version (node:22-alpine), not latest, so builds do not change by surprise. Several FROMs make a multi-stage build: build in one, copy only the result into a small final one.
tip.RUN: Runs while the image is built and bakes the result into it. Chain related commands with && so they share one layer, and clean caches in the same command.
tip.COPY: Brings files from your build context (or from another stage with "Copy from") into the image. Copy dependency files first and the rest later so Docker reuses its cache.
tip.ADD: Like COPY, plus downloading URLs and unpacking archives. Prefer COPY unless you need that.
tip.ENV: Stays in the image and in every container made from it. Never put passwords here.
tip.ARG: Exists only while building, but is visible in the image history. Not for secrets.
tip.WORKDIR: Creates the folder if needed and makes it the current one for the next steps and for the container. Always use an absolute path.
tip.EXPOSE: Only documents the port; it does not publish it. You publish ports when you run the container.
tip.USER: Run as a normal user, not root, so a flaw in the app does not give control of the container.
tip.CMD: What runs when the container starts, and what "docker run image something" replaces. Prefer the exec form so the app receives stop signals.
tip.ENTRYPOINT: The fixed program of the container; CMD then supplies its default arguments.
tip.HEALTHCHECK: Docker runs this command periodically and marks the container healthy or unhealthy, so you know the app really answers.
tip.VOLUME: Marks a folder whose data should outlive the container. Docker creates an anonymous volume for it if you do not mount one.
tip.LABEL: Free-form metadata, for example the image title or source repository.
tip.STOPSIGNAL: Signal sent to ask the app to stop (default SIGTERM).
tip.SHELL: Changes the shell used by shell-form commands (default /bin/sh -c).
tip.ONBUILD: Delayed instruction: it runs when someone builds another image FROM this one.

dotnetPublish.name: .NET: publish

aspnetPort.name: ASP.NET Core: port

dotnetCultureInvariant.name: .NET: invariant globalization

nonRoot.name: Run as non-root
nonRoot.desc: Uses the app user that .NET images already provide.

wgetHealthcheck.name: Health check with wget
wgetHealthcheck.desc: Lets Docker mark the container unhealthy when /health stops answering.

copyFromBuild.name: Copy the published app
copyFromBuild.desc: Brings the build stage output into the final image.

wizard.title: Dockerfile wizard

dotnet-blazor.name: Blazor WebAssembly
dotnet-blazor.desc: Static client app published and served by nginx.

node.name: Node.js app
node.desc: Install dependencies once, run as the node user.

python.name: Python app
python.desc: Pip requirements cached in their own layer.

go.name: Go service
go.desc: Static binary in a tiny final image.

fields.extraProjects: Other projects it references (one per line)

hints.project: Path from the build context root, e.g. src/Api/Api.csproj
hints.assembly: Leave empty to use the project file name
hints.extraProjects: Listed so the restore layer stays cached until dependencies change
hints.flavor: Alpine is small and has a shell; chiseled is the smallest and has none
hints.healthPath: Only Alpine has wget for the check

wizard.files: Also adds to the build context: {{files}}

notes.context: The build context must contain your solution or project folders: pick the project folder on the right.
notes.port: The app must listen on port {{port}} (ASPNETCORE_HTTP_PORTS is set for you).
notes.noTools: This image has no wget or curl, so there is no HEALTHCHECK; monitor the app from outside.
notes.noShell: Chiseled images have no shell: you cannot open a terminal inside the container.
notes.blazorClient: A Blazor WebAssembly app (client only). For Blazor Server use the ASP.NET Core recipe.

folder.title: Project folder
folder.hint: Send a folder from your computer as the build context (bin, obj, .git and anything in .dockerignore are left out). Without one, the build only sees the extra files below.
folder.tooBig: The folder is larger than 500 MB after .dockerignore.

swarm.title: Swarm
swarm.intro: Docker Swarm runs services replicated across one or more machines. Start a new cluster on this engine or join an existing one.
swarm.advertiseHint: IP other machines use to reach this one. Leave empty to detect it.
swarm.locked: This swarm is locked. Enter the unlock key to use it.
swarm.notManager: This node is a worker: manage the swarm from a manager node.
swarm.publishedWarning: A published port opens on every node of the swarm, on all interfaces.
swarm.removeServiceBody: Its tasks stop and the service disappears. Volumes are not touched.
swarm.removeNodeBody: The node leaves the cluster list. A node that is still running must be drained or left first.
swarm.removeStackBody: All the services of the stack are removed.
swarm.secretHint: The value is sent once and cannot be read back, not even by admins.
swarm.removeItemBody: Services that use it keep running until they are updated.
swarm.tokensWarning: Anyone with a token can add a machine to this cluster. Rotate it if it leaks.
swarm.autolockHint: With autolock the managers need an unlock key after a restart, so the cluster's secrets are not readable on disk.
swarm.leaveHint: This node stops being part of the cluster. Its services stop.
swarm.leaveBody: This node leaves the swarm and its services stop. This cannot be undone.
swarm.leaveZones: {{count}} overlay zone(s) are left without a cluster: {{names}}.
swarm.leaveServices: {{count}} service(s) stop here and the cluster creates them again on other nodes, if any remain: {{names}}.
swarm.leaveDataSafe: Data is not touched: volumes stay on this server's disk and standalone containers keep running.
swarm.leaveLastManager: This is the last manager: leaving dissolves the cluster. To keep it, promote another node to manager first.
swarm.leaveUnknown: This engine is not a manager, so Nautix cannot list what would be affected.

plugins.hint: Plugins add volume, network or log drivers. They run with elevated access on the host: install only plugins you trust.
plugins.privilegesTitle: This plugin asks for these permissions on the host:
plugins.removeBody: An enabled plugin is disabled first. Volumes or networks that use it stop working.

dns.title: DNS
dns.intro: Give your own names (for example app.home.lab) an IP address. Containers and machines that use your DNS container as their resolver will find them; every other name is forwarded to the upstream DNS.
dns.needServer: You need a DNS container first
dns.needServerBody: Deploy dnsmasq or CoreDNS from the palette (Topology → DNS) and it will show up here, ready to edit.
dns.unsupported: Found, but Nautix has no adapter for these yet (it can edit dnsmasq and CoreDNS from the palette):
dns.notRunning: The DNS container is stopped: start it to apply or test records.
dns.domainHint: Also covers its subdomains (db.app.lab → same IP as app.lab).
dns.clash: That name already has an address of the same type.
dns.applyHint: Writes the records into the container and restarts it (about a second without DNS).
dns.rejected: The DNS server rejected the records
dns.pickContainer: Use the IP of a container

manageApply.restart: Applying restarts the container (about a second without DNS).
manageApply.reload: Applying reloads the server by itself, with no downtime.

dns.firstApply: This server cannot start without its configuration: press "Save and apply" and Nautix writes it and starts the container.
dns.subdomainsNote: A name also answers for its subdomains.
dns.targetHint: An IP address, or a container name: Nautix looks up its current IP every time you apply, so it keeps working if the container is recreated.

exposure.title: Who can reach port {{port}}
exposure.addressHint: An address of this machine, for example its LAN or VPN IP.

help.address: Bound to one address of the host, for example your LAN or a VPN.
help.open: Bound to 0.0.0.0. Anyone who can reach this machine can reach the port.

exposure.recreate: Docker cannot rebind a running port: the container is recreated with the same settings (a short interruption). If the new one cannot start, the original is put back.
exposure.intro: Every port a container publishes on this machine and who can reach it. Open ports come first.
exposure.openCount: Open ports: {{count}}. Anyone on any network this machine is on can reach them.

guard.title: Port guards
guard.intro: Decide which networks may reach a published port, enforced by the host's firewall (iptables or nftables) for any protocol, not only HTTP. Rules take effect through a small privileged helper; Nautix itself stays unprivileged.
guard.helperBody: The helper is a separate container that runs on the host with network access to its firewall. It holds no data and opens no port: it asks Nautix for the rules and applies them.
guard.tokenOnce: This token is shown only now. Run the command below on the host; creating another token replaces this one.
guard.helperNote: If Nautix serves HTTPS the command already accepts its certificate for this loopback connection. Emergency switch on the host: docker exec nautix-guard node dist/guard-helper.js --panic
guard.allowHint: Addresses or networks such as 10.0.0.0/24. Everyone else is dropped.
guard.unresolved: container stopped or port not published: nothing is enforced
guard.disableBody: Every rule is removed and all published ports are reachable again by whoever could reach them before.
guard.trial: New rules are on trial. If you do not keep them in {{seconds}} s they are rolled back automatically.
guard.onTrial: Rules applied on trial: keep them within 60 seconds
guard.helperError: The helper could not apply the rules: {{error}}
guard.lockoutTitle: These rules may cut your own access
guard.lockoutBody: Your address is not in the allowed list of at least one rule, or a rule guards Nautix itself. You have 60 seconds to keep the rules; if you lose access they roll back by themselves. Apply anyway?
guard.note: Rules apply to traffic that Docker forwards to published ports (DOCKER-USER chain). With Docker Desktop or rootless Docker the helper cannot reach the host firewall.

env.title: Environment of {{name}}
env.recreate: Docker cannot change a running container's variables, so it is recreated with the same settings (a short interruption). The new one has to stay up (or pass its health check) or the previous one is put back.

apply.rolledBack: The change was rolled back: the previous container is running again.

bindings.dragHint: Drag to another container to bind them
bindings.title: Bind {{app}} to {{service}}
bindings.name: Name
bindings.nameHint: Names the settings, for example ConnectionStrings__Orders or ORDERS_URL.
bindings.cannot: These two cannot be bound yet. Check that the service is on a network you created.
bindings.secretNote: The service's password is copied into the app's environment, so anyone who can inspect the app can read it. Passwords are masked here.
bindings.recreate: The app is recreated to receive the settings; if it does not come up healthy, the previous one is put back and nothing is bound.
bindings.removeBody: {{app}} loses {{variables}} and is recreated. The network it joined stays.

zones.title: Zone {{name}} as a document
zones.intro: The whole zone as one YAML document. Edit it and the plan on the right shows exactly what would change; nothing runs until you press Apply, and every change that recreates a container is rolled back by itself if the new one does not come up.
zones.secrets: Environment values appear here in clear text, as they are in the containers. Only admins can see this page.
zones.inSync: The zone already matches the document. Nothing to do.
zones.allowRemovals: Also remove services that are not in the document
zones.applyFailed: The zone was not fully applied
zones.driftHint: What is running no longer matches the last applied document

action.update-service: Update {{service}} ({{fields}}): it is recreated and rolled back if it fails
action.replace-service: Replace {{service}} ({{fields}}): remove it and create it again

notes.networkInternalIgnored: The network {{zone}} already exists with a different isolation setting; it is not changed.
notes.anonymousVolumeLost: {{service}} has volumes without a name: replacing it loses their data.
notes.removesService: {{service}} is running but is not in the document.
notes.nameTakenOutside: The name {{service}} belongs to a container outside this zone.

cluster.nodesSummary: {{nodes}} node(s) · {{managers}} manager(s) · click one to highlight its tasks
cluster.haWarning: With {{count}} manager(s) the cluster cannot lose one and keep deciding. Three is the usual minimum.
cluster.nodeDown: No answer: its tasks were created again on other nodes.
cluster.focusHint: Read-only. To create or change services use the Swarm tab.
cluster.readOnly: Cluster view · read-only · refreshed every few seconds
cluster.notManager: This engine is a swarm worker, and a worker cannot list the cluster. Connect Nautix to a manager.
cluster.locked: The swarm is locked. Unlock it to see the cluster.
cluster.inspectorEmpty: Select a service to see where its copies run.
cluster.whereHint: Swarm spreads the copies over the active nodes unless the service is pinned or limited under Where it runs.

appearance.title: Appearance
appearance.accentHint: A fine detail for selection, links, zones and focus. Buttons stay white (dark) or black (light). Red, green and yellow are not available because they mean error, ok and warning. A second, related color (shifted toward teal) paints the overlays and, as a gradient, a few details: the selected node, the active tab and the edge of the inspector.
appearance.hueMoved: moved away from red, green or yellow
appearance.reduceTransparencyHint: Solid panels, no blur or glass. Also applied automatically when your system asks for it.

swarmCanvas.dialogTitle: Add a service to the plan
swarmCanvas.dialogHint: Nothing is created yet: the service is drawn dashed on the canvas and applied with the rest of the plan.
swarmCanvas.nameTaken: That name is empty, invalid or already used by a service or a change in the plan.
swarmCanvas.global: One copy on every node (global) instead of a number of replicas
swarmCanvas.portsHint: A port is reachable by the other services of the network without publishing it. Publish only what must be open to the outside.
swarmCanvas.publishedWarn: A published port opens on every node of the swarm, on all interfaces.
swarmCanvas.envHint: One KEY=value per line. Values are sent to the cluster and never shown again.
swarmCanvas.looseHint: Services on no overlay network. Drag a service onto an overlay box when creating it to put it there.
swarmCanvas.emptyOverlay: Drop a template here to create a service on this overlay.
swarmCanvas.empty: No services yet. Drag a template onto an overlay box, or create an overlay with New network.
swarmCanvas.plannedHint: Planned: it does not exist yet. It is created when you apply the plan.
swarmCanvas.globalNoScale: A global service has one copy per node: there is nothing to scale.
swarmCanvas.reviewHint: Changes are applied one by one. If one fails or the service does not start, everything done by this plan is undone.
swarmCanvas.rollbackFailed: These could not be undone and need a look in Resources, Swarm: {{steps}}
swarmCanvas.rolledBack: {{count}} change(s) undone: the cluster is as it was.
swarmCanvas.placementHint: Pinning keeps a service on one node: the only way to keep it next to its volume. The limit per node spreads copies.
swarmCanvas.volumesPinned: The volume is created on that node and the data stays there. Back it up from Volumes.
swarmCanvas.volumesNeedPin: A volume lives on the node where a copy runs. Without pinning, a copy that moves to another node starts with an empty volume: pin the service to a node.
swarmCanvas.noSecrets: There are no secrets yet. Create them in Swarm, Secrets: each one appears inside the container as a file.
swarmCanvas.imageHint: A new image rolls out one copy at a time. If it does not start, the engine puts the previous one back.
swarmCanvas.rollback: Roll back to the previous version
swarmCanvas.rollbackBody: The service goes back to the settings it had before its last update (image, networks, placement). Copies are replaced one at a time.
swarmCanvas.removeWarn: Removed last and not undoable: {{names}}. Its volumes and secrets stay, but its settings cannot be rebuilt from here.
swarmCanvas.bindHint: The first one receives the connection settings of the second as environment variables, so it can reach it by name over the overlay. Nothing changes until you apply the plan.
swarmCanvas.bindDrag: Drag to another service to bind them
swarmCanvas.bindNameInvalid: Letters and numbers, starting with a letter.
swarmCanvas.bindRolls: Applying updates the first service one copy at a time; if the new copies do not start, the engine puts the previous settings back.
swarmCanvas.healthHint: A command that runs inside the container; while it fails the copy counts as unhealthy and is replaced.
swarmCanvas.healthEnable: Check the copy with a command
swarmCanvas.resourcesHint: A limit caps what a copy may use. A reservation is set aside for it on a node: the scheduler will not place a copy where it does not fit.
swarmCanvas.policyHint: How a new image or a change rolls out and what happens when it goes wrong.
swarmCanvas.policyEditHint: Only changes how future updates roll out: no copy is replaced now.
swarmCanvas.noConfigs: There are no configs yet. Create them in Swarm, Configs: each one appears inside the container as a file.
swarmCanvas.portsEditHint: The list of ports that open on every node. Changing it replaces the copies one at a time.
swarmCanvas.volumesEditHint: Taking a volume out does not delete it, and adding one creates it on the node where a copy runs. Changing it replaces the copies one at a time.
swarmCanvas.envEditHint: Names only: Nautix never shows the values. Setting a name that exists replaces its value.
swarmCanvas.overlayHint: Docker cannot edit a network in place. To change it, create another one and move the services.
swarmCanvas.overlayNotEmpty: Move or remove its services first.

mounts.title: Mounted folders
mounts.hint: Maps a folder of this machine into the container (host folder : folder inside).

invalid.source: Use an absolute path on this machine, like /srv/data.
invalid.target: Use an absolute path inside the container, like /data.

docker-socket.name: Docker socket
docker-socket.text: This mounts the Docker socket. Whatever runs in this container can control Docker and, through it, the whole machine: it is the same as giving it root on the host.

host-root.name: Whole disk
host-root.text: This mounts the root of the machine's disk. The container will be able to read and change every file on the host.

sensitive-path.name: Sensitive folder
sensitive-path.text: This mounts a system folder (such as /etc, /root or Docker's own data). The container will be able to read it and, unless read-only, change it.

mounts.accept: I understand the risk and want to mount it anyway

bulk.confirmBody: This removes: {{names}}. It cannot be undone.
bulk.forced: {{count}} running container(s) will be stopped by force.
